title: Donna And Joe

jokes.text: orchids are Donna's favorite flowers, and she's my favorite flower.
jokes.setup: Joe explains that orchids will be in the pews because they're Donna's favorite flowers.
jokes.punchline: He pivots to calling Donna his 'favorite flower' — a sweet but slightly corny romantic declaration.
jokes.explanation: A warm, slightly cheesy romantic line that works because it's so earnest. Gets a gentle laugh from the sincerity, but it's not particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: We're having orchids at the wedding because, like an orchid, Donna is exotic, rare, and absolutely beautiful.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: Also like an orchid, she requires very specific conditions to thrive, and if you mess up even slightly, she will kill you.

jokes.text: Do you think this is my first time working a side job as a wedding planner for a former co-worker?
jokes.setup: Craig is managing Donna's wedding as a side job; someone questions him about the orchids.
jokes.punchline: Craig's wounded sarcasm implies this absurd scenario has happened before, but then immediately caves: 'No? I'm so sorry.'
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: the absurd implication that Craig does this regularly, then the instant deflation. Very Craig-specific — his explosive confidence collapsing into apology is signature character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking about us, and I realized that we're actually pretty cute together.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Yeah, we are. And I'm gonna enjoy this before one of us dies or realizes what a terrible mistake this is.

jokes.text: I mostly have my rage problem under control, but planning is very stressful. Please avoid my trigger words: 'flowers,' 'schedule,' 'vows,'
jokes.setup: Craig admits to having a rage problem but reassures everyone it's mostly under control.
jokes.punchline: He then lists his 'trigger words' — which are every single word associated with a wedding, making the reassurance meaningless.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation structure. The setup promises control, then immediately demolishes it. The list itself is the joke — every word is generic wedding vocabulary, making Craig's 'trigger words' indistinguishable from the job description. High quotability, great character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: Do you know anything about wedding planning?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Well, I once organized a funeral for a possum that died in my garage, so yes, I know everything about wedding planning.

jokes.text: 'bride,' 'groom,' 'food,' 'love,' 'happy,' 'church,' 'event,' 'wedding,' and 'Craig.'
jokes.setup: Craig's list of trigger words continues beyond the previous beat.
jokes.punchline: The list ends with 'Craig' — his own name is a trigger word for himself — followed by instant self-directed apology.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the trigger words escalation. 'Craig' being on the list is the perfect button — he's triggered by his own existence. The immediate 'I am so sorry, Craig. I'm sorry, I'm sorry' turns it into a triple beat. This is exceptional character comedy — absurd, perfectly structured, and utterly specific to Craig. Earns its high score.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm sorry for my outburst. I have a rage problem.

jokes.text: — And I love you like a sister. — Ew.
jokes.setup: Donna tells April she chose her as Maid of Honor because she's become one of her best friends and loves her like a sister.
jokes.punchline: April's instinctive, flat 'Ew' — rejecting the warmth entirely.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — one word does all the work. April's anti-sentiment reflex is entirely in character and the single syllable lands harder than a longer response would. Great structural compression.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm warning you, there are some trigger words. The list includes basically everything related to weddings, plus Craig's name.

jokes.text: The Meagles are a cold-blooded crew of judgmental grudge-holders.
jokes.setup: April describes Donna's family in a talking-head confessional.
jokes.punchline: The clinical, almost admiring description of them as 'cold-blooded' grudge-holders frames them like a dangerous gang.
jokes.explanation: A solid talking-head setup that efficiently characterizes the Meagle family threat level. Works because of April's deadpan delivery framing it as an objective threat assessment.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, Craig. I didn't mean to say your name.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: It's okay, April. I know it was an accident.

jokes.text: My cousin Winnie once forgot to use a coaster at my grandpa's house, and he wrote her out of his will.
jokes.setup: April is illustrating the Meagles' grudge-holding reputation.
jokes.punchline: The extreme disproportionality of the punishment — disinherited for a coaster — plays as dark absurdism.
jokes.explanation: Good specificity — 'Winnie' and 'coaster' make this feel like a real family story. The absurd severity is the joke and it lands cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: You know what? I care about you. You're like a sister to me.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Gross. Why would you say that? Now I have to go rinse my ears out.

jokes.text: The last four Meagle family Pictionary tournaments ended at the hospital.
jokes.setup: Continuing the pattern of Meagle family dysfunction stories.
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'four' and 'Pictionary' makes this a perfectly absurd image — a board game so competitive it requires medical attention, repeatedly.
jokes.explanation: The number 'four' does heavy lifting — it's not once (accident) or 'every time' (hyperbole) but four, which implies a pattern they're well aware of and apparently haven't stopped. Excellent economy and a very quotable image.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I need to name the centerpieces something ridiculous. How about LeVondrious?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's not a centerpiece name, that's a person's name.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Exactly. It's perfect.

jokes.text: Legally, no more than three Meagles are allowed on an international flight together.
jokes.setup: The Meagle danger stories are escalating with each beat.
jokes.punchline: This implies their family has caused enough international aviation incidents that there's an actual legal cap — a regulation specifically written about this family.
jokes.explanation: The peak of the Meagle escalation trilogy. The bureaucratic specificity — an actual legal limit on a family's air travel — is wonderfully absurd. The joke works because it implies consequence without explaining the incident, letting the imagination do the work. Among the best jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'll handle the family drama. I'm very good at compartmentalizing emotions and weaponizing them against people I love.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Which is why it disturbs me that I actually care about you guys.

jokes.text: But they give great gifts. Gotta get that flatware.
jokes.setup: Three escalating horror stories about the Meagles reaching dangerous/absurd extremes.
jokes.punchline: April's attitude completely reverses — the gifts outweigh all of it. The mundanity of 'flatware' is the button.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button to the Meagle monologue. The pivot from 'no more than three on an international flight' to 'but gotta get that flatware' is a great misdirection. The specificity of 'flatware' over 'gifts' makes it funnier — she's already mentally cataloguing the silverware.

jokes.text: Tommy, I was at the nail salon and I picked up some geranium hand cream. Do you wanna try it? Warm it up, please.
jokes.setup: Ron Swanson — hyper-masculine, anti-grooming — is at what appears to be a casual hangout with Tom.
jokes.punchline: Ron enthusiastically accepts hand cream and instructs Tom to 'warm it up' — a completely domestic, feminine-coded ritual delivered with total Ron seriousness.
jokes.explanation: Wonderful character inversion. Ron Swanson's intense masculinity contrasting with the complete casualness of his hand cream enthusiasm is perfectly observed. 'Warm it up, please' — the politeness and the specificity make it. High character integration score because this only works with Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: The Meagles are so petty. One time at a country club, Ben's ball landed on their cart path. A CART PATH. You know what they did? They called the club president, demanded we pay for a new cart, and made us sit at a different table for dinner.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Wait, there's more. The coaster from my drink left a ring on their glass table. Just a small ring. Barely visible. Gayle screamed like someone had murdered her dog. They hired a furniture restoration specialist. A specialist. For a coaster ring. The bill was $800.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Did they make you pay?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Of course they did. And then they sent us a framed photo of the restored table with a note that said 'Please be more careful next time.' Next time! Like I was going back to their house voluntarily.

jokes.text: As Donna's Butler of Honor, I'm going all out. Baby blue brocade. As a surprise, I got a matching dress for Lucy.
jokes.setup: Tom announces his grand gesture — matching outfits for him and Lucy at the wedding.
jokes.punchline: The confidence with which Tom presents this romantic disaster as a winning move, framed as a 'Butler of Honor.'
jokes.explanation: Tom's oblivious romantic overconfidence is well-established and this is a solid instance of it. 'Butler of Honor' is a nice Tom-ism. The real payoff comes later though — this is setup for the Lucy storyline.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: One time we played Pictionary and my uncle drew something that looked like a hot dog. My cousin thought it was a gun and tackled him through a glass coffee table. He needed 47 stitches.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: That's a Meagle family tradition.

jokes.text: — And do you believe Lucy will be happy with this gift? — 100%! We're so in sync.
jokes.setup: Ron, the one person who knows Tom already accidentally told Lucy he wants to marry her, hears Tom brag about being 'in sync' with Lucy.
jokes.punchline: Ron's question is loaded — he knows Tom is about to crash — but Tom is blissfully unaware. The dramatic irony is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Works primarily on dramatic irony — rewatch value is high because you know Ron is watching a disaster unfold. The '100%!' is funnier knowing what we know.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: The family is so problematic they're legally restricted from flying.

jokes.text: Bully for you, son. More importantly, do you have tri-tip for tonight? Because if not I brought my own.
jokes.setup: Tom has just shared that he feels like he's finally found his forever person and would 'marry her tomorrow.'
jokes.punchline: Ron dismisses the emotional revelation entirely with 'Bully for you' and pivots to the most pressing issue: meat availability. He even came prepared.
jokes.explanation: 'Bully for you' is a perfectly Ron turn of phrase — slightly formal, slightly dismissive — and the food priority is deeply character-specific. 'Because if not I brought my own' is the button that makes it great: Ron's contingency planning is for meat, not emotions.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: The Meagles are terrible people. But you know what? They pay me in cash, they never ask questions, and they tip like they're trying to make a dead relative proud. So I tolerate them.

jokes.text: I love weddings. Good food, the celebration of romantic love, and most of all, churches. Say what you will about organized religion, those bastards knew how to construct an edifice.
jokes.setup: Ron giving a talking-head about why he loves weddings.
jokes.punchline: The list prioritizes churches above love, then the punchline is specifically about architecture — his appreciation of religion is entirely structural/material, and 'those bastards' is a perfectly Ron way to pay an architectural compliment.
jokes.explanation: 'Those bastards knew how to construct an edifice' is a genuinely great line. The surprise that 'most of all' is churches (not food or love) and then the deflation that it's only about the buildings is perfectly constructed. 'Those bastards' as a term of architectural respect is the kind of specific Ron Swanson word choice that earns high scores.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. Is that hand cream? Warm it up first.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I don't put anything on my hands that isn't at least 98.6 degrees.

jokes.text: Okay, monsters. Mommy and Daddy have to pack because we are going to a hotel.
jokes.setup: Leslie is talking to her young children.
jokes.punchline: Calling her own toddlers 'monsters' in a completely matter-of-fact tone — equal parts exhausted and affectionate.
jokes.explanation: A gentle parenting joke — calling toddlers 'monsters' is familiar territory but delivered with the right Leslie energy. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm not the Best Man, I'm the Butler of Honor.

jokes.text: Do you think I could have 30 seconds? That's all. — She's fading.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to give their nanny Roz a pep talk but the children are clearly causing chaos.
jokes.punchline: She desperately asks the nanny if she could have 30 seconds of quiet. Ben's aside 'She's fading' treats Leslie's breakdown like a sporting event.
jokes.explanation: 'She's fading' is the better half of this exchange — Ben's sportscaster read on his wife's stress is an affectionate, efficient joke. Works as a quick beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm going to surprise Lucy with a dress I picked out myself.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Tom, that's a terrible idea.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Why? I have great taste.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're wearing a shirt with a picture of a boat on it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's a very nice boat.

jokes.text: I love you more than Ben. I do. If Ben left me, I would be sad, but I would get through it. But if you left me, I would never recover.
jokes.setup: Leslie is effusively praising her nanny Roz to make sure she won't quit.
jokes.punchline: Leslie explicitly ranks Roz above her husband in importance — and then doubles down with detailed emotional forecasting. The escalation from 'I love you more than Ben' to the full impact assessment makes it land harder.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's frantic sincerity pushing past acceptable social limits is classic character comedy. The emotional calculus she does — grieving each scenario — is very funny and very Leslie. The tag 'Thanks. That helps.' from Roz is the button.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why would you do that?

jokes.text: Thanks. That helps.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just told her nanny she'd 'never recover' if Roz left, explicitly prioritizing Roz over her husband.
jokes.punchline: Roz's flat, slightly hollow 'Thanks. That helps.' — delivered with the dry affect of someone who has processed a lot of Leslie Knope.
jokes.explanation: A perfect button to joke 18. The ambiguity of whether it genuinely helps or is just a polite non-response is what makes it work. Maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, are you sure Lucy is going to like this dress?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, Ron, Ron. I have never been more confident about anything in my life. This dress is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's a size 0 and she's clearly a size 8.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: She'll grow into it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's neon green.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's retro.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: There's a stain on it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Vintage patina.

jokes.text: I'm so used to packing for them I almost put in diapers for myself.
jokes.setup: Leslie is packing for their hotel stay.
jokes.punchline: Her autopilot has gotten so parent-brained that she nearly packed adult diapers for herself.
jokes.explanation: A relatable parenting joke delivered with the right casual delivery. Not groundbreaking but functional and specific enough.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We're so in sync, I bought her a dress without asking and she loved it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Next thing I know, we're getting married.

jokes.text: She'll just say what she always says... 'Leslie, would you consider running for state senate or Congress?' And I'll say, 'Jen, thank you very much, that's very flattering, but I love my job.' The whole world is my park.
jokes.setup: Leslie explains why she doesn't need to answer Jen's call — she already knows the whole conversation.
jokes.punchline: 'The whole world is my park' — Leslie's grandiose self-mythology delivered with complete sincerity. It's simultaneously inspiring and absurd.
jokes.explanation: 'The whole world is my park' is quintessential Leslie Knope — the self-aggrandizing mission statement delivered without a hint of irony. Character-specific and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I love weddings. Mostly the churches. I love the smell of the wood, the beautiful stained glass, the cool marble floors. I love kneeling, the sitting, the standing, the kneeling again. But mostly I love the kneeling.

jokes.text: All three of them just bumped into each other and broke everything you own.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just said 'things aren't that chaotic' regarding their ability to manage a political campaign.
jokes.punchline: Ben delivers the perfect counter-evidence in real time — a live demonstration of their chaos — with the matter-of-fact timing of a news ticker.
jokes.explanation: Structural perfection — the scene immediately contradicts Leslie's claim. The specificity of 'bumped into each other' (the triplets colliding) and 'broke everything you own' (implying total destruction) delivered deadpan while Leslie is mid-sentence is excellent timing.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I love the outdoors. And I hate most people. But I love their churches. Beautiful buildings. It's too bad they're full of bastards.

jokes.text: You know Gayle gives me a gift each and every day. I got the greatest gift of all — being married to you.
jokes.setup: Tom is about to give Lucy the matching dress. Jerry/Garry observes approvingly and mentions Gayle gives him a gift every day.
jokes.punchline: Jerry/Garry's completely earnest, unironic happiness — delivering a cheesy romantic line with absolute sincerity — is the joke. In a show where Jerry is perpetually humiliated, his blissful domestic contentment is both sweet and funny.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Jerry/Garry is completely unironic while everyone around him is being knowing and sardonic. His genuine happiness is the punchline. Works on character level.

dialogue.speaker: Roz
dialogue.line: The kids and I had such a great time today! We went to the park, then we got ice cream, then we played games, then we sang songs, then we danced, then we played more games!

dialogue.speaker: Roz
dialogue.line: Please. I'm begging you. Just 30 seconds of quiet. That's all I need.

jokes.text: Control yourselves, Gergiches!
jokes.setup: Jerry/Garry and Gayle have just exchanged a sweet romantic moment.
jokes.punchline: Jerry/Garry, aware they're being watched, scolds himself and Gayle to 'control themselves' — as if their warmth is scandalous.
jokes.explanation: Sweet self-awareness. 'Gergiches!' as a collective noun for their couple-unit is charming. The joke is that their love is so robust it must be restrained.

dialogue.speaker: Roz
dialogue.line: I need thirty seconds of quiet.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay. And... go.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's like watching a dying person try to remember the name of their first dog.

jokes.text: I normally don't get involved in people's personal affairs, but something about a wedding... I'll just say it. Tom is quite taken with you. He said he'd marry you tomorrow.
jokes.setup: Ron is pulling Lucy aside at the rehearsal dinner, opening with his characteristic reluctance to involve himself.
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'I normally don't get involved' is immediately undercut by him doing exactly that — and then delivering Tom's most intimate feelings in the most formal possible register ('quite taken with you').
jokes.explanation: 'Quite taken with you' is perfect Ron diction — formal, slightly Victorian — applied to modern romantic feelings. The self-contradiction in 'I don't get involved but here I am' is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Roz, you're such an amazing caregiver. Honestly, I love you more than I love Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, you're really great with the kids.

jokes.text: Let's just make, like, three more, so that each one of them can have a friend.
jokes.setup: Leslie has told Ben not to joke about more kids.
jokes.punchline: Ben doubles down with a 'logical' proposal: three more kids so each existing child has a friend — a solution so insane it loops back to sincere.
jokes.explanation: The internal logic is funny — three more kids so each kid gets a friend — which would result in six toddlers. Ben presenting this as a reasonable solution is good character comedy. The escalation from 'don't joke' to 'no seriously, three MORE' works.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I love Roz more than Ben. If I lost Roz, I would have no one to complain to about Ben. I need her.

jokes.text: My life is amazing.
jokes.setup: Jen has just called Leslie's life 'gross.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate, reflexive, genuine counter — not defensive, just corrective. Her certainty is unshakeable.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button to joke 30. Three words that completely characterize Leslie's resilient self-image. Economy score is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Almost packing diapers for myself out of habit.

jokes.text: You guys live in Pawnee, Indiana. Where do you have to go? Putting up a new scarecrow?
jokes.setup: Leslie says they have to go and can't talk right now.
jokes.punchline: Jen's contemptuous rural Pawnee joke — implying their only possible obligation is agrarian.
jokes.explanation: Good Jen character work — her coastal contempt for Pawnee is well-deployed. 'Putting up a new scarecrow' is specific enough to land.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I love my job because I get to protect America's greatest natural treasures. Every day, I wake up knowing that I'm preserving these magnificent landscapes for future generations. I'm not just a parks department employee—I'm a guardian of the American spirit, a steward of the land, a—

jokes.text: Whoa! What was that? That was huge! Hang on, this is Congress you're talking about, like, where bills become laws.
jokes.setup: Jen has just revealed the candidate she wants to run isn't Leslie — it's Ben.
jokes.punchline: Ben's awed, overwhelmed response to being nominated for Congress — specifically 'where bills become laws' — is the wide-eyed civics lesson recall of a man genuinely surprised by his own potential.
jokes.explanation: 'Where bills become laws' is the joke — it reduces Congress to a Schoolhouse Rock summary, which perfectly captures Ben's stunned, processing state. Character-specific to a former mayor who grew up in politics but can't quite believe this is happening to him.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Things aren't that chaotic.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We've got everything under control.

dialogue.speaker: Child 1
dialogue.line: Ahhhhh!

dialogue.speaker: Child 2
dialogue.line: Help!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Never mind.

jokes.text: We're talking about the House of Representatives, Ben. You might be overqualified.
jokes.setup: Ben says he's not qualified for Congress.
jokes.punchline: Jen's straight-faced, slightly contemptuous 'You might be overqualified' — a dig at Congress's actual competence level.
jokes.explanation: Sharp, cynical political humor delivered with Jen's signature certainty. 'Overqualified' for Congress is a great institutional joke. Economy is excellent — she does a lot of satirical work in one word.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What happened here? Why is there a hole in the wall?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And why are all the books on the floor? And why is the couch upside down?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I was gone for twenty minutes. Twenty minutes!

jokes.text: Two of the three kids are showering in their pajamas, and most of Ben's ties are in the toilet.
jokes.setup: Jen is waiting for Ben's answer on whether he'll run for Congress.
jokes.punchline: Leslie provides a live chaos update — children showering in pajamas, ties in the toilet — as evidence that their lives are, in fact, chaotic.
jokes.explanation: Each specific detail is individually funny — pajama showers and toilet ties — but together they paint a picture of total domestic disintegration. 'Most of Ben's ties' implies multiple ties, in the toilet, concurrently. Good specific absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Gayle is the most beautiful, intelligent, talented woman I have ever known. She makes me want to be a better man. Every day with her is like a gift from God himself.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah, I'm sure the Dig Dug machine just unplugged itself right before I was about to beat his high score.
jokes.setup: Two characters are still arguing about a decades-old incident at what's apparently a party or gathering.
jokes.punchline: The highly specific arcade game grievance — Dig Dug! — being held for what sounds like years frames the Meagle grudge capacity perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Confirms and extends the Meagle grudge character work. 'Dig Dug machine just unplugged itself' as sarcasm is good — it reveals a multi-year conspiracy theory about a video game.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Hey! There are children present!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm calling the police. This is indecent exposure.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Get a room, you two. Better yet, get a bunker.

jokes.text: The Meagles are weird. The words that they say sound passive, but seem aggressive. I feel like there should be a term for that. Like, 'nicey-meanie.'
jokes.setup: Andy is reporting back on his observations of the Meagle family interactions.
jokes.punchline: Andy has independently discovered passive-aggression and named it 'nicey-meanie' — his oblivious reinvention of an established concept is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Nicey-meanie' is a great Andy Dwyer coinage — he's so earnest and unread that he's genuinely discovered passive-aggression for the first time and named it himself. The delivery of 'I feel like there should be a term for that' as sincere observation is perfect character comedy. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom said he wants to get married.

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.line: Really? That's surprising.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Yes. He told me in confidence, but I'm telling you immediately because I don't respect his privacy.

jokes.text: I just had to physically separate two 80-year-old men who were arguing about whether it was really Lena Horne in that grocery store in 1970.
jokes.setup: April is giving a status report on Meagle management.
jokes.punchline: The absurd specificity — Lena Horne, a grocery store, 1970 — combined with the octogenarian physical altercation paints a wonderfully ridiculous scene.
jokes.explanation: The historical specificity makes this feel real. The mental image of April physically separating elderly men over a 50-year-old celebrity sighting is vivid and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: What is that noise in the background?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh, those are my kids. They're playing.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Children? Ugh.

jokes.text: Or woman. I mean, equal rights. No, that doesn't apply.
jokes.setup: Ben is processing the idea of being a congressman.
jokes.punchline: Ben reflexively adds gender correction then realizes a congressman can, in fact, be a congressman regardless — his own correction was wrong. The self-contradicting allyship attempt makes him flustered.
jokes.explanation: A quick, smart beat — Ben's progressive instincts getting tangled up as he thinks out loud. The self-correction of the self-correction is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Where do we need to go?

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Oh, I assume there's a town square where everyone gathers to discuss harvests and compare yeoman accomplishments?

jokes.text: Ben has to run. I don't want to push it, because it might backfire, but he has to run. He would be good for America, good for the world. Ben should be the Royal Archduke Sultan Emperor of All Inhabitable Lands on Earth! I'm completely neutral.
jokes.setup: Leslie is in a talking-head saying she'll 'support Ben no matter what' and is 'completely neutral.'
jokes.punchline: She escalates from 'he has to run' to inventing the title 'Royal Archduke Sultan Emperor of All Inhabitable Lands on Earth' — a list of every head-of-state title she could think of — then snaps back to 'I'm completely neutral.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalation from 'completely neutral' to 'Royal Archduke Sultan Emperor of All Inhabitable Lands on Earth' is a perfect Leslie Knope arc in miniature. The title is funny because of its redundant accumulation of power words, and the snap back to 'I'm completely neutral' shows she has zero self-awareness. High character integration — this joke could ONLY be Leslie. Competes for the episode's top spot.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm not qualified for Congress.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Actually, I think you're overqualified.

jokes.text: You told Lucy I want to marry her? — Damn it, son, the small hamburgers.
jokes.setup: Tom confronts Ron about having told Lucy he'd marry her.
jokes.punchline: Ron's response to an emotional crisis is to withhold food as leverage. 'Damn it, son' registers frustration; 'the small hamburgers' is his only actual concern.
jokes.explanation: 'Damn it, son, the small hamburgers' is an excellent Ron line. The micro-aggression of being called 'son,' the immediate pivot to hors d'oeuvres, and the bathos of 'small hamburgers' (rather than, say, 'the food') — all very Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The absurd specific details of the destruction

jokes.text: Even though I've known Lucy for years, and can see myself spending a life together with her, having children, walking the grounds of Tommy's Bahama — a private island I'll eventually buy — that's way in the future, man. — Don't call me 'man.'
jokes.setup: Tom is explaining that he does have feelings for Lucy but it's too soon to express them.
jokes.punchline: The fantasy escalates from children to 'walking the grounds of Tommy's Bahama — a private island I'll eventually buy' — then Ron's only objection to the entire speech is being called 'man.'
jokes.explanation: 'Tommy's Bahama' (riffing on Tommy Bahama the brand) as a future private island name is perfectly on-brand for Tom's aspirational delusions. Ron's correction being solely about 'man' vs. any of the actual content is a great reversal — he's accepted the island but won't be called 'man.'

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: They're so passive-aggressive. They do this thing where they're nice to your face but then they're mean behind your back. I call it being a 'nicey-meanie.'

jokes.text: Don't serve this man. No more food until he fixes his giant disaster he's created.
jokes.setup: Ron is deploying the only leverage he has over Tom — food.
jokes.punchline: The gravity of 'Don't serve this man' as a consequence for a romantic miscommunication is delightfully disproportionate. Ron treating food access as a moral sanction.
jokes.explanation: Callback to the food leverage established earlier. Ron's use of catering access as moral enforcement is perfectly in character — it's the one power he can actually wield at this event.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking about running for Congress. I want to make sure I'm inclusive and represent everyone. So I'm going to start saying 'congressperson' instead of 'congressman.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's great, Ben!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I'm going to say 'chairwoman' or 'chairperson' depending on the situation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Very thoughtful.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm also going to refer to my constituents as 'you guys and dolls.'

jokes.text: Hey, guys. / Nope, too hard.
jokes.setup: Jen tells Ben to start campaign mode — meet and greet, make everyone feel interesting and important. Ben approaches two random people.
jokes.punchline: His opening 'Hey, guys' prompts an immediate 'Nope, too hard' from Jen, suggesting even that minimal effort failed
jokes.explanation: Efficient and well-timed. The joke is in the immediacy — Ben barely opens his mouth before being shot down. 'Too hard' is wonderfully dismissive for such a simple greeting. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm completely neutral about Ben running for city council. I have no opinion whatsoever.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But if he does run, he's going to be amazing. He's the smartest, most talented, most attractive man in the entire world. Vote for Ben Wyatt!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But like I said, I'm neutral.

jokes.text: Uh, hi, Mr. and Mrs. Meagle, I presume? — I am Mr. Meagle, but we're divorced. — I'm Grace Callahan. — Well, I'm sorry, Ms. Callahan. — It's Doctor Callahan. — Well, I hope that you are a podiatrist or a dentist, because I seem to have a case of foot-in-mouth disorder.
jokes.setup: Ben approaches Donna's parents with a classic presumptuous married-couple greeting.
jokes.punchline: Each correction makes it worse, until Ben lands a pun on 'foot-in-mouth' as his recovery — which is itself a bit cringe-y but delivered with Ben's characteristic earnest awkwardness.
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed escalating awkwardness. Each response digs deeper — divorced, wrong name, wrong title — until Ben commits to the pun as a recovery. The pun itself is the extra layer of cringe that makes it a Ben Wyatt joke specifically.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, man, I need your help with something.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Don't call me 'man.' I'm not your man. I'm a free citizen with my own name.

jokes.text: Hey, everybody. Meagles! I am not screwing around. Lauren, no more discussion of Majorca. Brian and Gloria, stop making Horatio feel bad that your daughter went to Yale. No one gives a shit. And, Ginuwine? Get it together.
jokes.setup: April has been briefed on troublemakers and is now addressing the Meagle family directly.
jokes.punchline: April's blunt, specific grievance list — including telling Donna's family members 'no one gives a shit' about Yale and addressing a family member named Ginuwine (apparently after the singer) — is perfectly April.
jokes.explanation: April managing the Meagles like a disappointed principal is very character-specific. 'No one gives a shit' about Yale at a family event, combined with 'Ginuwine' as an actual family member's name, is the kind of specific absurdism Parks does well.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm scared, man. What if this doesn't work out? What if I'm not good enough for her?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You called me 'man.' We're good.

jokes.text: Easy peasy. Lemon sneezy.
jokes.setup: Andy apparently helped defuse a Meagle situation by comforting someone named Ginuwine.
jokes.punchline: Andy's version of 'easy peasy lemon squeezy' — he's either mishearing or innovating with 'lemon sneezy.'
jokes.explanation: 'Lemon sneezy' instead of 'lemon squeezy' is a perfect Andy Dwyer malapropism. It's almost right, which makes it funnier than being completely wrong. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: If Tom doesn't straighten up, I'm cutting off his food supply. A man needs to learn consequences.

jokes.text: I am a liar. — What? — Well, no, I am not a liar. I have never lied about anything in my life. Though I suppose you could construe camouflage as a lie.
jokes.setup: Ron is trying to apologize to Lucy for accidentally oversharing Tom's feelings.
jokes.punchline: Ron opens by declaring himself a liar, immediately denies it, then goes off on a philosophical tangent about whether camouflage is deception — all while Lucy waits for the actual point.
jokes.explanation: Ron getting stuck on his own ethics mid-apology is great character comedy. The camouflage tangent is very Ron — it's military, philosophical, and completely off-topic. Could only be Ron Swanson.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Ben Wyatt. I'm running for City Council.

dialogue.speaker: Voter
dialogue.line: We don't care.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, well, I'm just going to go home and lie in bed and think about this.

jokes.text: Tom wanted to convey that he likes you a great deal. So he said that he could imagine marrying you. And living on an island with your kids. — Wait, now we're on an island? With kids? Plural?
jokes.setup: Ron is relaying Tom's feelings to Lucy as diplomatically as possible.
jokes.punchline: Lucy's incremental horror at each new detail — island, then kids, then plural — mirrors the audience's reaction to how far Ron has gone.
jokes.explanation: The callback to Tom's private island fantasy lands here through Ron's clinical retelling. Lucy's escalating alarm — island, kids, plural — is well-structured comedic escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Your daughter is amazing, and I promise to take care of her. Also, I think I'm having a stroke because I can't feel my face.

jokes.text: Watch out for those riding lawnmowers, man.
jokes.setup: Ron is walking away from the Lucy conversation, having caused more confusion than resolution.
jokes.punchline: A completely non-sequitur safety warning — Ron's parting advice to Lucy is about lawn equipment.
jokes.explanation: The total non-sequitur is very Ron — it implies he was already thinking about something else entirely and this practical warning is his genuine goodbye. Efficiently strange.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so we're treating family members like criminals to be rounded up?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's the plan.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I love it. It's like a fun, family-oriented police state.

jokes.text: Ever since we had our kids, it only takes, like, one sip of wine. I feel so good and 'condifent.' Con... I feel 'condifent.'
jokes.setup: Ben reveals they're both drunk; Leslie confirms she's a complete lightweight post-kids.
jokes.punchline: Leslie tries to say 'confident' and can't — the repeated failed attempt at the word is funnier than just being drunk. 'Condifent' is a specific kind of drunk.
jokes.explanation: 'Condifent' is a very specific, accurate depiction of one-glass-of-wine drunk. The repetition — she tries twice and fails both times — adds to the escalation. Highly quotable as a state of being.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I need you to understand something, Ginuwine. I don't care about your feuds with the other Meagles. I don't care about your drama. What I care about is that you show up on time, do your job, and don't make my life harder than it already is.

dialogue.speaker: Ginuwine
dialogue.line: But April—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not done. You're going to sit down, shut up, and listen to what I'm telling you right now, because if you don't, I will make sure that every single member of your family regrets the day they were born.

jokes.text: Toast it, baby. Roast it and toast it till it's brown on both sides.
jokes.setup: Ben is about to give a toast; Leslie enthusiastically encourages him.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's drunk escalation of 'give a toast' to 'roast it and toast it till it's brown on both sides' — mixing metaphors into full culinary nonsense.
jokes.explanation: The escalating food metaphor from 'toast' to 'brown on both sides' is drunk-Leslie logic at its best — she's extending the metaphor past its breaking point with total confidence.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Easy peasy lemon squeezy.

jokes.text: What? It's you! I love you! You're my sexy roommate. We love each other.
jokes.setup: Ben is giving what's supposed to be a toast about marriage, but he's drunk.
jokes.punchline: His description of marriage as 'you're my sexy roommate' — the most reductive possible definition — delivered as a sincere emotional revelation.
jokes.explanation: 'Sexy roommate' as drunk-toast marriage philosophy is both very funny and oddly sweet. The stutter-step framing ('What? It's you!') mimics actual drunk-person epiphany delivery well.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, no, no, Lucy, what Ron meant to say is that I don't lie. I just tell alternative facts. There's a difference. Lying is when you say something that's not true. Alternative facts are when you say something that's not true, but you say it with more confidence.

jokes.text: Whoo! He's talking about me. — Yes, I am, babydoll!
jokes.setup: Ben is giving a drunk toast and Leslie is watching.
jokes.punchline: Leslie claiming 'he's talking about me' as if it's not obvious — and Ben confirming it mid-toast — is a sweet, funny mutual drunk moment.
jokes.explanation: Sweet character beat. Not a sophisticated joke but their mutual drunk sincerity is charming. 'Babydoll' as Ben's drunk term of endearment is specific.

jokes.text: And I am Ben Wyatt, and I very much approve this message!
jokes.setup: Ben closes his drunk toast.
jokes.punchline: The political ad sign-off — 'I very much approve this message' — applied to a rehearsal dinner toast, foreshadowing his actual campaign announcement.
jokes.explanation: The political sign-off as a drunk toast button is perfect — it works as pure comedy in the moment, and it's also thematically resonant with the Congressional plotline. Rewatch value is high because it's an accidental preview of Ben's actual campaign.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, just a heads up — if you ever see a possum in your house, don't try to pet it. They have opposable thumbs and they will steal your wallet.

jokes.text: You want me to shut that down? — No, I like it. — Let the little man dance. — Hey!
jokes.setup: After Ben's toast, someone has apparently started dancing (presumably Ben).
jokes.punchline: Ron's indulgent 'Let the little man dance' and Ben's offended 'Hey!' at being called a 'little man.'
jokes.explanation: Ron's 'little man' as affectionate condescension is good — he says it with the warmth of someone watching something they're barely tolerating. Ben's 'Hey!' confirms he's heard it and objects to the diminutive.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm very... confibent. No wait, confident. Con-fi-dent. Confibent. I meant confident!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why is this word so hard? Con-FI-dent. Confibent. Ugh, confident!

jokes.text: Last night was so fun. But my head died. — Mine's filled with concrete.
jokes.setup: The morning after the rehearsal dinner, both Leslie and Ben have hangovers.
jokes.punchline: 'My head died' and 'filled with concrete' — two colorfully specific descriptions of a hangover that escalate from bad to worse.
jokes.explanation: The hangover descriptions are vivid and specific enough to be fun. Works as a transition beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm feeling very... confadent. No wait, confidant. Con-fi-dent. Confadent.

jokes.text: Jen posted the campaign ad. It's everywhere. I'm running. — How could she do this to— Oh, God, I'm remembering things. We called Jen last night, didn't we?
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie wake up to discover Jen has posted a campaign ad.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's horror mid-sentence dissolves as she starts remembering — and realizes they CALLED Jen and apparently made this happen themselves.
jokes.explanation: Good escalating discovery joke — the horror of the situation is compounded by realizing they caused it. The mid-sentence cutoff as the memory surfaces is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Marriage is like having a best friend who you can also have sex with. You're just sexy roommates. Sexy roommates who file taxes together and occasionally argue about whose turn it is to take out the garbage.

jokes.text: I also called 867-5309 100 times.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are cataloguing what they did while drunk.
jokes.punchline: Among the serious revelations, Leslie admits she drunk-dialed the famous Tommy Tutone number 100 times.
jokes.explanation: '100 times' is the detail that elevates this from a typical pop culture reference joke. It's not a single drunk dial — it's a sustained, repetitive campaign. The subsequent callback where someone sings the song makes it better.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm the sexy roommate!

jokes.text: All those kids keep you up all night? — I'm so happy with my choices.
jokes.setup: Jen is gloating at the hungover, exhausted Leslie and Ben.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate, zombified 'I'm so happy with my choices' — delivered while clearly suffering — is the exact opposite of convincing.
jokes.explanation: A callback to Leslie's unshakeable self-belief, now undercut by visible suffering. The contrast between her physical state and her declaration is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, when I first met you, I thought you were crazy. You had all these wild ideas and no filter. But over the years, I realized that's what I love about you. You see the world not as it is, but as it could be. So today, I'm asking the people in this room to join me in voting for Leslie Knope for wife of the year. And I promise you, together, we can make our marriage great again.

jokes.text: I know I left you a message last night, but I really do think you should have checked with me before throwing me into this. — No, Ben, I'm sorry, you left me four messages last night.
jokes.setup: Ben confronts Jen about going public with the campaign without his consent.
jokes.punchline: Ben thought he left one message — Jen reveals it was four, with 'very specific policy positions.'
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — Ben thinks he gave one hesitant call, Jen reveals four enthusiastic policy messages. The gap between how he remembers himself and what he actually did is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Let the man dance. He's like a young, gangly foal learning to use his legs for the first time. It's beautiful, really.

jokes.text: I want to come out strong on education. Then I'll tack hard into fiscal responsibility.
jokes.setup: Jen reads back Ben's drunk policy positions from his voicemails.
jokes.punchline: Ben's drunk self had coherent, well-formed campaign positions — he was more competent at campaign strategy while intoxicated.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that drunk Ben was a more decisive candidate than sober Ben. 'Tack hard into fiscal responsibility' is specific enough to be funny — it's not generic, it sounds like real policy language delivered by someone who knows what they're talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I called 867-5309.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Over and over again.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: All night.

jokes.text: ♪ 8-6-7-5-3-0-9 ♪ — I love that song. — ♪ Jenny, I've got your number ♪ — Hey, babe, it's ringing!
jokes.setup: Jen mentions Ben's four messages; Leslie is reminded she called 867-5309.
jokes.punchline: Ben spontaneously starts singing the song, Leslie joins in, then Leslie realizes she's dialed it again.
jokes.explanation: The callback works beautifully — the mention triggers the song, the song triggers the dial, and 'Hey, babe, it's ringing!' confirms Leslie has done it again despite knowing better. Good comic structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Jen, hey, it's Ben. Look, I've been thinking about us, and I realize now that we need to pivot our messaging strategy to realign with core demographics and synergize our key value propositions.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Also, I'm drunk and I miss you. We should leverage this moment to restructure our relationship framework going forward.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Call me back. Let's touch base about our vertical integration.

jokes.text: Oh, you guys are gonna fit in so great in Washington. Most of Congress is drunk, all of the time.
jokes.setup: Jen learns they made the campaign decision while drunk.
jokes.punchline: Rather than being concerned, Jen reassures them that drunkenness is standard operating procedure in Congress.
jokes.explanation: 'Most of Congress is drunk, all of the time' is a genuinely sharp political joke delivered with Jen's breezy authority. The reassurance framing is perfect — she's not scandalized, she's welcoming them to the club.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I may have called and requested it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You what?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I called the bar and requested our song. I wanted to hear it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's so romantic. And also completely insane.

jokes.text: I'm just gonna go spend my time doing exactly what I want to do, because I don't have children. Bye, guys.
jokes.setup: Jen wraps up the meeting.
jokes.punchline: Jen's parting shot is an explicit celebration of her childfree freedom, timed perfectly to exit while Ben and Leslie sit in their exhaustion.
jokes.explanation: Jen's unapologetic anti-parent posture is one of the episode's consistent comedy engines. The 'because I don't have children' as explicit explanation is the key — she's not implying it, she's stating it as the direct cause of her freedom.

jokes.text: Michelle... You were my best friend from childhood. Until we lost touch 'cause you thought your college boyfriend was into me. — He was. — I never gave him the time of day.
jokes.setup: Donna's pre-wedding speech to her bridesmaids takes an unexpectedly complicated turn with Michelle.
jokes.punchline: Michelle's flat, unapologetic 'He was' — confirming the accusation — forces Donna to defend herself at her own wedding.
jokes.explanation: The casual confirmation 'He was' is excellent — Michelle has waited years to say this, and she picks the moment Donna is most exposed. The timing is cringe-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt. Please, continue with what you were saying. I'm genuinely interested in hearing your thoughts on this matter.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You know, I really respect your expertise here. I wouldn't want to overstep or impose my views. What would you recommend?

jokes.text: But the doctors once told you you were never going to walk again. So this should be easy, right?
jokes.setup: Donna is asking Michelle to suppress any jealousy at the wedding.
jokes.punchline: Donna's 'motivational' speech invokes Michelle's past medical trauma as a comparator — essentially saying 'you overcame paralysis, you can handle not being jealous.'
jokes.explanation: Wonderfully dark. Donna using Michelle's most traumatic medical experience as a behavioral benchmark is exactly the kind of Donna confidence that makes her character special. 'So this should be easy, right?' — the casual application of the comparison is the killer beat.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Your boyfriend wasn't really into you.

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: Yeah, he wasn't.

jokes.text: Wow, what a complicated tapestry that is.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just witnessed Donna's entire exchange with Michelle — the jealousy, the confirmation, the medical history weaponized as motivation.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's stunned, diplomatic 'What a complicated tapestry that is' — the verbal equivalent of backing away slowly.
jokes.explanation: 'Complicated tapestry' is the kind of diplomatic non-comment that's perfect for Leslie — it says nothing while acknowledging everything. Very quotable as a reaction to overwhelming social information.

dialogue.line: The completely absurd name 'Typhoon'

jokes.text: Hi, I'm Typhoon. — Typhoon, I am interested, but now is not the time. Michelle, get the bouquet. You're skating on very thin ice.
jokes.setup: A new person introduces themselves to Donna at a chaotic moment.
jokes.punchline: Donna's 'I am interested, but now is not the time' — managing intrigue while simultaneously threatening Michelle — captures Donna's multi-tasking authority.
jokes.explanation: The two-target management — the stranger gets curiosity deferred, Michelle gets a warning — in rapid sequence is good Donna character work. 'Skating on very thin ice' applied to a bridesmaid at the bride's wedding is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Typhoon
dialogue.line: I am Typhoon, a spiritual guide and healer.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Cool. I'm interested.

jokes.text: I couldn't help but notice, from afar, that you are both acting like weirdoes. I further suspect you have not yet talked about what happened.
jokes.setup: Ron approaches Tom and Lucy, who have been awkwardly avoiding each other.
jokes.punchline: 'Acting like weirdoes' as Ron's formal observational report is perfectly clinical. 'I further suspect' as if issuing a finding is very Ron.
jokes.explanation: Ron's formal register applied to social observation is consistently funny. 'I further suspect' is the key phrase — it has a report-filing gravity that's wonderfully misapplied to noticing two people being awkward.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: The key to a good relationship is honesty. You have to be completely honest with your partner.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Honesty? That's like... a weird quirk of yours, right?

jokes.text: I am sorry if I caused a problem. Because the two of you make a good team. If you'll excuse me, I missed out on the food, and was denied a fascinating conversation about Michigan limestone. But I'll be damned if I don't properly honor the expression of romantic love.
jokes.setup: Ron gives his wise advice to Tom and Lucy about communicating their feelings.
jokes.punchline: Ron lists his grievances — missed food, denied limestone conversation — then pivots to committing to properly honor romantic love, as if it's an obligation he takes seriously despite the personal cost.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Ron treating missed food and a limestone conversation as equivalent personal sacrifices, then committing to honor love as a solemn duty, is perfectly Ron Swanson. 'I'll be damned if I don't properly honor the expression of romantic love' is a great line — the formal register and the implication that love is a procedural obligation he won't shirk earns the high score. This joke also rewards the whole episode: it's a callback to both the food and the limestone, and it reveals Ron's actual sweetness under layers of self-interest.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Lucy, I love you. I want to spend the rest of my life with you.

dialogue.speaker: Lucy
dialogue.line: Aww, that's sweet. Is this before or after you liquidate my assets?

jokes.text: Ron does this weird thing where he says exactly what he means. You just have to ignore him.
jokes.setup: Lucy is confused by Ron's directness.
jokes.punchline: Tom's advice to 'ignore' Ron for saying exactly what he means — implying that honesty is the social aberration here.
jokes.explanation: A sharp meta-observation about Ron as a character, delivered by someone who knows him well. 'Says exactly what he means' as a social disorder is a wonderful inversion, and 'you just have to ignore him' is the perfect, absurd prescription.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: I've learned so many new things about you, Donna. Like, did you know that Fleetwood Mac's 'Rumours' album was actually written about you?

jokes.text: Well, I'm only dating you for the free dresses, so...
jokes.setup: Tom has just made a vulnerable declaration of his feelings — he's all in, even if it's too soon.
jokes.punchline: Lucy deflates the sincerity with a joke about materialistic motives — then the 'so...' implies she's actually reciprocating.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured joke that also does emotional work. The tension-diffusing humor ('free dresses') cuts the vulnerability without rejecting it, and the trailing 'so...' is the real punchline — implying she's also all in. Economical and character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hi Roz, it's Leslie Knope from Parks and Rec. I'm calling because I heard there was an incident at the DMV with some zebras and children?

dialogue.speaker: Roz
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's right. Some zebras got loose in the waiting area.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Were the children okay? I mean, were they... interacting with the zebras?

dialogue.speaker: Roz
dialogue.line: Unfortunately, yes.

jokes.text: Hey, Roz. Oh, okay. We have the zebras. Tell the kids not to worry, they're coming back home. Also, we want to give you a raise, and anything you want to take from our house.
jokes.setup: Leslie takes a call from the nanny Roz during the wedding.
jokes.punchline: 'We have the zebras' as a casual, mid-wedding crisis — delivered as if 'we have the zebras' is a sentence that needs to be said at all.
jokes.explanation: The sheer mundanity of 'we have the zebras' as a phone call during a wedding is excellent absurdism. The offer of 'anything you want to take from our house' as nanny retention suggests this is a recurring negotiation.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: What are your qualifications for this position?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, I've worked in government for over a decade. I've balanced budgets, managed crises, and I've even dealt with a current zebra situation that I really don't want to get into.

jokes.text: How in the world am I supposed to run for office? Our lives are like one big unexpected stuffed zebra emergency.
jokes.setup: Ben has just witnessed the zebra phone call and is questioning his fitness for office.
jokes.punchline: 'One big unexpected stuffed zebra emergency' — Ben's characterization of their life as a specific category of disaster. 'Stuffed zebra' implies they're toy zebras, but raises more questions than it answers.
jokes.explanation: 'Stuffed zebra emergency' is the kind of phrase that sticks. The 'unexpected' qualifier implies there's a category of expected zebra emergencies, which is funnier. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I just want to say, Leslie and Ben, you two are perfect together. You complement each other. But I have to be honest, I'm not here to talk about your love. I'm here to talk about my business success. Rent-A-Swag has really taken off. We're in three malls now. Three! I've also started a second company called Entertainment 720, which is going to revolutionize the way people think about entertainment. Ben, your campaign is great, but let me tell you about my business plan...

jokes.text: Honey, you have never been neutral on anything in your life. You have an opinion on pockets. / Yes, I think they should all be bigger.
jokes.setup: Ben challenges Leslie's claim to neutrality about his congressional run
jokes.punchline: Leslie confirms the pocket opinion without hesitation — both validating Ben's point AND making a completely sincere argument about pocket size
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best exchanges. The setup is perfect: Ben makes a specific, quirky example (pockets) to illustrate Leslie's strong opinions. Leslie's immediate and sincere 'Yes, I think they should all be bigger' is the ideal response — she confirms she has the opinion AND the opinion itself is characteristically earnest and policy-adjacent. The joke works on multiple levels: it's funny, it's character-defining, it touches on a genuine issue (women's pocket sizes), and Leslie's conviction makes it even better. The economy is exceptional — eight words that reveal so much. Justifies the 8.5+.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, did someone just call him Jerry? His actual name?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what, I'm going to call him Garry from now on. It's like Jerry, but with a G. It's a power move.

jokes.text: Besides, I just read an article on two-minute micro-naps, and the science on them is very promising.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just made a passionate case for Ben running for Congress despite their chaotic lives.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's sleep strategy for managing a congressional campaign and triplets is 'two-minute micro-naps.' She's read an article.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's manic research-based optimism applied to an impossible logistical problem is character-specific. 'The science on them is very promising' as a serious claim about two-minute naps is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Thank you. Thank you so much for calling me Garry again. It means the world to me.

jokes.text: Reporters ambush Ben holding zebras while asking about his congressional run
jokes.setup: Ben is in the middle of a zebra emergency when reporters suddenly appear asking about his congressional announcement
jokes.punchline: Ben attempting to give a serious political statement while physically holding zebras — and referencing them in his answer ('I'm dealing with an actual problem right now. Okay? Which, by the way, is what I do for a living.')
jokes.explanation: The visual of a congressional candidate being interrogated while holding zebras is inherently funny. The callback to the zebra emergency paying off as the backdrop for a genuine political announcement is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: LeVondrious
dialogue.line: I'm back, and I know what you did.

jokes.text: I'm dealing with an actual problem right now. Which, by the way, is what I do for a living.
jokes.setup: Ben is being peppered by press questions while holding zebras.
jokes.punchline: Ben's pivot from 'I have a zebra problem' to 'this is literally my job, solving problems' — using the absurd present situation as evidence of his qualifications.
jokes.explanation: This is a great comedic pivot that also serves as genuine character development. Ben using the zebra emergency as an unintentional campaign speech metaphor — 'I'm dealing with an actual problem, which is what I do for a living' — is both funny and true. The structure is excellent: the absurdity of the situation grounds the speech, making his improvised announcement feel earned.

dialogue.speaker: LeVondrious
dialogue.line: I have traveled far and wide, through deserts of despair and oceans of regret, to be here on this momentous day. And I bring with me a seven-tier wedding cake, because I heard there would be cake.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, babe, that was so hot.
jokes.setup: Ben has just delivered an impromptu, passionate campaign announcement while holding zebras.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate, unfiltered 'that was so hot' — political competence as an aphrodisiac.
jokes.explanation: Leslie finding competence and civic passion attractive is deeply in character. The immediate delivery — no pause, no context — is the joke. Works as a relationship beat and a character punchline.

jokes.text: I gotta say I kind of miss the Meagle drama. I thought for sure somebody was gonna do something crazy. But everybody's just nice and chill.
jokes.setup: Donna thanks April for managing the wedding perfectly.
jokes.punchline: Donna admits she actually wanted some drama — this is setup for the LeVondrious arrival.
jokes.explanation: Works primarily as setup for the LeVondrious callback. Donna's admission that she misses drama is characterful but the real payoff is elsewhere.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! What are you doing? That's the microwave!

dialogue.speaker: LeVondrious
dialogue.line: I'm destroying it!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Well, how am I supposed to make my popcorn?

jokes.text: Wyatt, why didn't you tell us you're running for congress? — Well, we didn't want to steal your thunder. — Steal my thunder? I'm sorry, have you seen how I'm wearing this dress?
jokes.setup: Donna finds out Ben is running for Congress at her wedding.
jokes.punchline: Donna's indignant response to the idea that Ben's news could 'steal her thunder' — her confidence in her own look is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: 'Have you seen how I'm wearing this dress?' is an excellent Donna line. The confidence is absolute — no congressional announcement can compete with her dress game. High character integration and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: LeVondrious
dialogue.line: Wait, you set this whole thing up? You got me to come here?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I wanted to see you two go at it. Meagle drama is the best drama.

dialogue.speaker: LeVondrious
dialogue.line: That's... actually kind of genius.

jokes.text: — To Ben. — Donna and Joe. — To me. I own my own restaurant and several other properties. That's always worth celebrating.
jokes.setup: A toast round at the wedding celebration.
jokes.punchline: Tom hijacks the toast circle to toast himself, with a complete inventory of his holdings delivered as if this is standard behavior.
jokes.explanation: Tom's braggadocious self-toast is very in character. 'Several other properties' as an unspecified flex, and 'that's always worth celebrating' as a confident closer, is good Tom Haverford energy.

jokes.text: Who's Garry? — Oh, I think that's supposed to be me. — Ha ha. That's your new name. Garry. — Garry! Garry! Garry!
jokes.setup: Someone at the party calls Jerry by the name 'Garry.'
jokes.punchline: It's revealed that Jerry's real name is actually Garry — and after 30 years, the group is now chanting it as a new joke, not a correction.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best gags. The revelation that Jerry's real name is Garry — after years of being called Jerry — and that his coworkers immediately adopt it as another way to mock him is wonderfully dark. But Jerry's 'Oh, boy, I'm blessed' response — genuine gratitude that they're finally using his real name, even as a joke — is perfectly heartbreaking and sweet. Exceptional character integration.

jokes.text: Garry is my real name. Yes, after 30 years, my coworkers are finally going to call me by my real name. Oh, boy, I'm blessed.
jokes.setup: Jerry/Garry's coworkers are chanting 'Garry!' as if it's still a joke.
jokes.punchline: Garry's talking-head reaction: 30 years of being called the wrong name, and now his real name is also a joke — and he's grateful.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best single joke. The pathos is immense: 30 years of the wrong name, and now the right name is delivered as a punchline, and Garry is still grateful. 'Oh, boy, I'm blessed' is the perfect ending — it's entirely sincere, which makes it funnier AND sadder. The joke earns its emotional weight through the show's entire run of Jerry mistreatment. Character integration is nearly perfect — this could only be Jerry/Garry, this could only be Parks and Recreation.

jokes.text: Now it's time for a surprise musical guest, one of my all-time favorites... me.
jokes.setup: Donna announces a surprise musical guest at her wedding.
jokes.punchline: The buildup implies a celebrity; the reveal is Donna herself, who presents this with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: 'One of my all-time favorites... me.' The pause and the reveal is classic misdirection structure. Donna's self-regard as a musical artist is entirely in character and the delivery is perfect.

jokes.text: I hope you saved a slice of that cake for your estranged brother LeVondrious! What's up, girl? Didn't expect to see your baby bro at your wedding, huh? Well, I'm here... despite what you did to me all those years ago. — What I did? — This is because of what you did. — Oh, you must be referring to the microwave incident. — Yeah. — Don't worry. I brought it back.
jokes.setup: The estranged brother LeVondrious crashes the wedding with a dramatic grievance about a years-old incident.
jokes.punchline: The microwave incident is the cause of years of family estrangement — and LeVondrious's resolution is 'I brought it back.' He's returned the microwave.
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff to the entire Meagle grudge theme. The callback perfectly delivers on the 'cold-blooded grudge-holders' setup from the episode's cold open. The punchline — 'I brought it back' — is wonderfully bathetic. Years of family estrangement over a microwave, resolved by its return. The structure is near-perfect: dramatic buildup, blame exchange, and then the mundane prop as solution. High scores across the board.

jokes.text: Well. Now no one gets any popcorn.
jokes.setup: LeVondrious has returned the microwave — but apparently broken it in the process.
jokes.punchline: Donna's flat 'Well. Now no one gets any popcorn.' — accepting the new, worse status quo with total composure.
jokes.explanation: The button to the whole LeVondrious sequence, and one of the episode's best lines. 'Now no one gets any popcorn' is an extraordinary amount of comedy per word. The 'Well.' pause before it is the chef's kiss — Donna processing the situation before accepting it. The line is both deeply specific (popcorn!) and universally applicable as a statement of resigned acceptance. Near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: You said you wanted a little drama. — That's why I love you, girl!
jokes.setup: Donna expressed missing drama; April apparently arranged or allowed LeVondrious to attend.
jokes.punchline: April revealing she engineered the drama as a wedding gift, and Donna's delighted response.
jokes.explanation: A sweet and funny callback close — April used her maid-of-honor powers to deliver the drama Donna actually wanted. 'That's why I love you, girl!' is Donna's highest endorsement. Rewatch value is high because it recontextualizes April's management of the Meagles — she was managing them so she could deploy LeVondrious at the right moment.

tmdb_overview: Donna and Joe tie the knot, while April attempts to keep the wedding running smoothly. Ron creates an awkward situation between Tom and Lucy. Jen Barkley arrives at Ben and Leslie's house with an interesting opportunity.
insight: Donna's wedding delivers 78 jokes in 22 minutes—highest density since Season 4.
